title: Storyboard: Sunflowers are among my favorite flowers, and at this size, we can observe them closely
source:
Sunflowers are among my favorite flowers, and at this size, we can observe them closely. These flowers are typically pollinated by bees, but when bees aren’t present, they have a clever method to ensure pollination. The male part, the anther, curls inward to transfer pollen to the sticky female stigma. This process is called self-pollination.
In plants like Xanthium, the anther and stigma mature simultaneously, which facilitates self-pollination and is termed homogamy. Some plants, such as wood sorrel, produce small, inconspicuous flowers in late summer that lack fragrance. These bisexual flowers remain closed, and self-pollination occurs within the unopened flower—a process known as gynostogamy. In such plants, pollen is already positioned on the stigma to enable self-pollination.
Cross-pollination is encouraged in plants like papaya, which are dioecious, meaning male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Sunflowers, however, have bisexual flowers where the anther matures before the stigma, a process called pro-tandry. In contrast, custard apple flowers have stigmas maturing first, termed pro-togeny.
Some flowers, like pansies, have a hood covering the stigma, a structural adaptation called hercogamy. In orchids, pollen from the anther fails to germinate on the same flower’s stigma. Primrose exhibits heterostyle, with the stigma positioned at a different height than the anther. These adaptations promote cross-pollination.
Pollinators are attracted by scent, nectar, or mimicry, such as the bee orchid, which mimics a female bee to trick males into pollinating it. Keep exploring to learn more. Stay curious. We believe in you.
